question:
Points \(A,\) \(B,\) \(C,\) and \(D\) are distinct and lie, in the given order, on a straight line. Line segments \(AB,\) \(AC,\) and \(AD\) have lengths \(x,\) \(y,\) and \(z,\) respectively. If line segments \(AB\) and \(CD\) may be rotated about points \(B\) and \(C,\) respectively, so that points \(A\) and \(D\) coincide, to form a triangle with positive area, then which of the following three inequalities must be satisfied? \[ \begin{aligned} &\text{I. }x\lt\frac z2\\ &\text{II. }y\lt x+\frac z2\\ &\text{III. }y\lt\frac z2 \end{aligned} \]

[Figure 1](figures/1979_AMC_12_Q17_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
Rotation preserves each segment's length, so the useful first step is to identify the sides of the completed triangle. Since the original points occur in the order \(A,B,C,D\), we have \(0<x<y<z\), and
\[
BC=y-x,\qquad CD=z-y.
\]
Let \(T\) be the common position of the rotated points \(A\) and \(D\). Triangle \(BCT\) therefore has side lengths \(x\), \(y-x\), and \(z-y\).

A triangle with positive area satisfies all three strict triangle inequalities. Applying them gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
(y-x)+(z-y)>x
&\implies z>2x
\implies x<\frac z2,\\
x+(z-y)>y-x
&\implies 2x+z>2y
\implies y<x+\frac z2,\\
x+(y-x)>z-y
&\implies 2y>z
\implies y>\frac z2.
\end{aligned}
\]
The inequalities are strict because equality would place the three vertices on a line and give zero area. Thus I and II must be satisfied, and III is false. The answer is \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
